clinicalPearls: Autosomal recessive defect of mitochondrial electron transfer caused by variants in ETFA, ETFB or ETFDH, impairing flavoprotein-dependent transfer of electrons from many acyl-CoA dehydrogenases into the respiratory chain.
Because numerous dehydrogenases are affected simultaneously, there is combined blockade of fatty-acid, branched-chain amino-acid and lysine/tryptophan oxidation.
Severe neonatal forms may present with or without congenital anomalies, including cystic kidneys, dysmorphism and a distinctive odour, often with overwhelming hypoketotic hypoglycaemia and acidosis.
Later-onset (mild) disease presents as a lipid-storage myopathy with exercise intolerance, proximal weakness and episodic metabolic decompensation.
Urine organic acids show a characteristic pattern of glutaric and other dicarboxylic acids, and the acylcarnitine profile shows broad elevation of short-, medium- and long-chain species.
Many riboflavin-responsive cases, particularly those due to ETFDH variants, improve dramatically with riboflavin supplementation.
Acute management centres on reversing catabolism with generous carbohydrate and avoiding fasting; carnitine and riboflavin are used adjunctively.
Consider the diagnosis in any hypoketotic hypoglycaemia, unexplained metabolic acidosis, or lipid-storage myopathy across the age range.
reference.pathophysiology: Glutaric aciduria type 2, or multiple acyl-CoA dehydrogenase deficiency, arises from defects in the machinery that shuttles electrons from mitochondrial flavoprotein dehydrogenases into the respiratory chain. Electron transfer flavoprotein (ETF), a heterodimer of ETFA and ETFB, accepts electrons from at least a dozen acyl-CoA dehydrogenases and passes them via ETF dehydrogenase (ETF-QO, encoded by ETFDH) to coenzyme Q. Biallelic loss-of-function variants in any of these three genes impair reoxidation of the flavin cofactors of the upstream dehydrogenases, so their reactions stall. The consequence is simultaneous blockade of mitochondrial fatty-acid beta-oxidation, oxidation of the branched-chain amino acids, and lysine, tryptophan and sarcosine metabolism. During fasting or intercurrent illness the body cannot mobilise fat for energy, producing hypoketotic hypoglycaemia, energy failure and accumulation of numerous acyl-CoA intermediates that are exported as their carnitine and glycine conjugates and as dicarboxylic and glutaric acids. Lipid accumulates in muscle and liver, causing myopathy and hepatic steatosis. Because these dehydrogenases depend on flavin adenine dinucleotide derived from riboflavin, some variants, especially in ETFDH, destabilise the enzymes in a way that is partly corrected by supraphysiological riboflavin, explaining the riboflavin-responsive phenotype. The most severe neonatal forms may be accompanied by congenital malformations such as renal cysts, reflecting the metabolic disturbance during organogenesis.
additionalDifferentials: Isolated fatty-acid oxidation defects (medium- or very-long-chain acyl-CoA dehydrogenase deficiency)
Primary carnitine deficiency and carnitine cycle disorders
Urea cycle disorders and organic acidaemias presenting with encephalopathy
additionalInvestigations: Urine organic acid analysis showing glutaric and dicarboxylic aciduria
Plasma acylcarnitine profile by tandem mass spectrometry
Blood glucose, ketones, ammonia, lactate and blood gas during illness
ETFA, ETFB and ETFDH gene sequencing
Creatine kinase and, where indicated, muscle biopsy for lipid storage
Trial of riboflavin with biochemical and clinical response monitoring
redFlags: Hypoketotic hypoglycaemia with encephalopathy or reduced consciousness
Severe metabolic acidosis or rapid clinical deterioration during intercurrent illness
Cardiac dysfunction or arrhythmia suggesting metabolic cardiomyopathy
Rapidly progressive muscle weakness or respiratory muscle involvement
Neonatal presentation with congenital anomalies and overwhelming acidosis
reference.prognosis: Severe neonatal-onset disease, especially with congenital anomalies, often has a poor outcome despite treatment, whereas milder later-onset and riboflavin-responsive forms can improve substantially and remain stable with supplementation and avoidance of catabolic stress.
pitfalls: Missing riboflavin responsiveness and withholding a trial that could produce marked improvement
Allowing prolonged fasting during illness or fasting for procedures, precipitating decompensation
Interpreting the broad acylcarnitine elevation as several separate disorders rather than one combined defect
Overlooking the diagnosis in adults presenting as an apparently acquired lipid-storage myopathy
Assuming normal interictal biochemistry excludes the disorder, as abnormalities may be intermittent
references: Newborn screening and metabolic medicine guidelines
management: Trial riboflavin supplementation, as many cases, especially those due to ETFDH variants, are riboflavin-responsive with marked clinical improvement
Adopt a diet low in fat and protein with avoidance of fasting and frequent carbohydrate intake to reduce demand on the blocked flavoprotein-dependent pathways
Supplement with L-carnitine and consider coenzyme Q10 to support residual mitochondrial function
Manage acute metabolic decompensation with intravenous glucose to suppress catabolism and correct hypoglycaemia and acidosis
Monitor for the lipid-storage myopathy in later-onset disease and adjust activity and nutrition accordingly
Coordinate specialist metabolic and dietetic follow-up with monitoring of glucose, carnitine status and metabolic markers
Offer genetic counselling for autosomal recessive inheritance of ETFA, ETFB or ETFDH variants
